data.title: Middle East Eye: Death, displacement and disease: A young Gaza doctor on life under Israeli bombardment
data.author: Faisal Edroos
data.summary:
Death, displacement and disease: A young Gaza doctor on life under Israeli bombardment
Submitted by
Faisal Edroos
on
Fri, 10/02/2026 - 12:10
Maryam Youssef tells The Gaza Podcast why she volunteered at the Nasser Hospital, what it was like contracting chickenpox as bombs rained down around her and her struggle to process the trauma of war
Off
A young Palestinian doctor who survived Israel's genocidal war on Gaza has described what it was like confronting the burden of patient care almost immediately after graduating.
In the first episode of Middle East Eye's The Gaza Podcast, which was recorded inside the besieged enclave, Maryam Youssef described the horrors she experienced while volunteering - and living - at Nasser Hospital.
She recalls contracting chickenpox and being forced to isolate in a room for days as bombs rained down around her, and how she has struggled to process the trauma of surviving the conflict.
"I had chickenpox after two days [of starting work at the hospital]," Youssef told podcast host Hussam Tannera.
Asked how she continued working while infected, she said: "I basically locked myself in my room and I stayed there for four to five days."
"The first two days no one knew. On the third day, I think that's when people that I work with began to notice and they give me some meds."
Youssef said she began volunteering at Nasser Hospital shortly after her family was displaced for a second time, leaving her with nowhere else to go.
Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, like many other hospitals in the enclave, had been repeatedly targeted, besieged and raided by Israeli forces - most notably during a major siege in early 2024 and a deadly double-tap air strike in August 2025.
'I think I was hungry most of the time, just as everyone else was'
- Maryam Youssef, doctor
Thousands of Palestinians had sought shelter at the hospital after repeated Israeli evacuation orders, leaving them trapped in a constant state of fear and uncertainty, unsure where they could go

data.title: Middle East Eye: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of oil and diesel from reserves, Macron says
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
G7 to release up to 100m barrels of oil and diesel from reserves, Macron says
G7 countries plan to release up to 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel from strategic reserves over four months to ease global pressure on suuplies and prices amid the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, French President Emmanuel Macron said.
Members also agreed to keep diesel exports flowing within the group, with Macron saying they would impose “no ban” on those shipments.
“It has been agreed to continue coordinating actions to help facilitate the exit of shipments from the Strait of Hormuz,” Reuters quoted Macron as saying.
His comments follow US President Donald Trump’s announcement that Europe would immediately release a “massive” quantity of diesel from its reserves.
A G7 joint leaders' statement on the plan said: "We have agreed on decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks."

US and Israeli army officers walk in front of a US Patriot missile defence system during the joint Israeli-US military exercise 'Juniper Cobra' at the Israeli Hatzor Air Force Base, on 8 March 2018 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off
The US has deployed additional Patriot air defence batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar, as President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to resume attacking Iran.
The US sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility and another to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility, Axios reported Thursday.
The deployments are notable because Patriot batteries are in high demand worldwide, and the US has a limited supply. The US has just 33 batteries stationed at home and 27 batteries stationed overseas, according to the nonprofit Missile Defence Alliance.
The US’s allies, including Gulf states like Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, already operate their own batteries, but have relied on Washington for additional protection as they have borne the brunt of Iran’s retaliation for US and Israeli attacks.
Saudi Arabia is in a particularly difficult position with its energy infrastructure and cities coming under attack from Houthi fighters in Yemen and Shia militias in Iraq. The kingdom attributed an attack on its East-West Pipeline to the latter, although the Houthis have also attacked Yanbu, the kingdom’s main oil export port.
Gulf states felt sidelined by the US earlier this year when they faced intense Iranian barrages in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran. The US’s decades-old security umbrella that underwrote its relationship with the energy-rich Gulf has come under scrutiny as a result of the war.
